4.0.0.en: If by the divine Incarnation the Word of God came down to us to betroth us as a bride for Himself, and by His crucifixion He held the wedding feast, then by His resurrection He has justified us, so we became the risen bride who is without blemish. Therefore the Bridegroom praises her, seeing in her all beauty, and says to her:

4.0.1.en: "Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair!" [1].

4.0.2.en: Through the resurrection He bestowed upon the Church all spiritual beauty and power, of which St. Peter the Apostle speaks, saying: "According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue: whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust" (2 Pet 1:3-4). And the marks of this beauty are: 1. "Thine eyes are doves under thy veil (thy silence)" [1].

4.0.3.en: St. Abdosius says: [The eyes are beautiful as the eyes of a dove because she is in the likeness of the dove of the Holy Spirit who came down from heaven]. We saw before that the Lord likens His Church to the eyes of a dove, because as she looks continually upon the Holy Spirit, His image shines forth upon her eyes, so she has spiritual insight far from every earthly or carnal impression, and she is simple, seeking nothing but what is of God, loving like the dove, and resting only in the arms of the true Noah, as the dove did which went out from the ark.

4.0.4.en: As for their being under the veil, it is because the mysteries of the Spirit which the eyes of the Church behold cannot be understood or grasped by the world, so they remain for it as though under a veil!

4.0.5.en: The literal translation is "in thy silence," for the Church, her insight having been opened to behold the spiritual mysteries of God's love, stands in silence contemplating the surpassing works of God, and as St. John Saba says: [Whoever wishes to speak about the love of God proves his ignorance, because speaking about this divine love is not possible at all.

4.0.7.en: It is the language of the angels, and words find it hard to translate it...!

4.0.8.en: It is not for us, my Lord, to speak out of what is ours about what is Yours. But You speak in us about Yourself, and about all that is Yours, as it pleases You].

4.0.9.en: And perhaps He described the eyes as under the veil because the believers, however much they enjoy spiritual insight in this world, it is considered as though under a veil when compared with the vision in the eternal life, for the Apostle says: "For we know in part... for now we see in a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:9, 12). 2. "Thy hair is as a flock of goats couching on mount Gilead" [1].

4.0.10.en: If the Lord Christ is the head of the Church, then the Church is the hair surrounding the head, which lives upon it; without the head she is worth nothing and has no existence.

4.0.11.en: This is the people of Christ: it is like a flock of goats feeding on the high mount Gilead, the mountain of the lofty word of God which sets out with the hearts of the children of God toward heaven.

4.0.12.en: The higher the flock goes up the mountain, the more man sees it from afar in one unity, so that he cannot distinguish one from another... So when we arise with the Lord and are lifted up above through the word of salvation and enjoy His ecclesiastical care, to live in a heavenly spirit, the spirit of division and schism, whose causes are earthly thinking, the seeking of temporal honor and the love of the world, is removed from us.

4.0.13.en: When we arise with the Lord we ascend mount Gilead like a flock of goats gathering together on the summits, so that it is seen from afar like smooth, black, shining hair into which no gray enters, for the Lord renews our youth like the eagle's.

4.0.14.en: As for the description of the flock as couching on the mountain, it means sitting and resting in the word of God without haste, settled under God's care in tranquility.

4.0.15.en: As for His choosing mount Gilead, it is for many reasons:

4.0.16.en: a. On mount Gilead God appeared to Laban and warned him, saying: "Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad" (Gen 31:24)... So the believer feels assurance; no one can touch him...

4.0.17.en: b. The slopes of mount Gilead were distinguished by abundance of pasture, so it became a figure of the life of satisfaction, for when the Lord promised His people of old that He would deliver them from violent Babylon and bring them into satisfaction, He said to them: "And I will bring Israel again to his habitation, and he shall feed on Carmel and Bashan, and his soul shall be satisfied upon mount Ephraim and Gilead" (Jer 50:19), and in the Book of Micah it is said: "Let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old" (Mic 7:14).

4.0.18.en: c. In ancient times balsam grew in Gilead, known for its fragrant scent, which the ancient poets and historians used to praise at length, and which physicians used for healing wounds and diseases. Therefore it is written in Jeremiah the prophet: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? Why then is not the daughter of my people bound up?!" (Jer 8:22). It is as though on mount Gilead the true Physician, Jesus Christ, binds up the wounds of His people and heals their diseases with the balsam of His blood poured out on the Cross.

4.0.19.en: d. When Gideon entered into war with the army of the Midianites, thirty-two thousand of the people gathered for the war, but the Lord said to Gideon: "Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead" (Judg 7:3). So God does not care about a great number but seeks striving believers who know neither fear nor terror! This is the true Church of Christ, which has been given power to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy, living in complete confidence without fear.

4.1.0.en: 3. "Thy teeth are like a flock of shorn (sheep) that came up from the washing" [2].

4.1.1.en: It is fitting for the Church to have teeth, for she has grown and matured and the milk of teaching no longer suffices her, but she seeks its rich food, chewing it and digesting it in her life.

4.1.2.en: St. Augustine says that the teeth of the Church are her servants, who chew the food like nursing mothers and present it as milk to the little ones in the faith. These teeth are of different kinds, canines and molars... but they work for one end and in one spirit for edification.

4.1.3.en: With these teeth the Lord asked the Apostle Peter to eat the animals after they were slain, and not to call anything unclean or common. For the Church works continually, through her servants, to present the word of salvation to all, slaying the uncleanness of evil and chewing the pagan Gentiles and tearing apart their evil and errors until they become members of her body.

4.1.4.en: The servant is like the shorn sheep, whose wool is cut... that is, he cuts off from himself the thoughts and works of the flesh by the Holy Spirit who was given to him in the font of Baptism (the washing). For wool in the Holy Bible signifies the carnal life, therefore in the Old Testament the priests were forbidden to enter the sanctuary in garments made of wool, but their garments were to be of linen, a sign of the righteousness of Christ. As the Mosaic Law affirmed: "Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together" (Deut 23:11), "for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?!" (2 Cor 6:14-15).

4.2.s.en: 4. "Whereof every one beareth twins, and none is barren among them" [2].

4.2.0.en: In the natural child the teeth usually grow in the gums in pairs, and so God used to send His disciples, the teeth of the Church, two by two to preach, perhaps so that one may utter the word of preaching while the other prays for him, so that the word goes forth anointed with divine grace.

4.2.1.en: When St. Pachomius was asked why he allowed the monks to live in their cells two by two, he answered: because if one falls the other raises him up.

4.2.2.en: St. Augustine sees in the phrase "beareth twins" a reference to the two commandments that complete each other, "love of God" and "love of neighbor," for by them the Law and the Prophets are fulfilled (Mt 22:40). Meanwhile St. Cyril of Jerusalem sees that it refers to the double grace, that is, that man is perfected by water and the Spirit, or through the graces to which the two Testaments, the Old and the New, pointed.

4.2.3.en: St. Jerome comments on this phrase, saying: [If none among them is barren, then all must have breasts filled with milk, able to say with the Apostle: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you" (Gal 4:19), "I have fed you with milk, and not with meat" (1 Cor 3:2).

4.2.4.en: Finally we can say that whoever has enjoyed the word of salvation by way of the pure teeth of the Church, that is, her true servants, must not remain barren but bear more than one, that is, have double fruit. Let him imitate the Samaritan woman, who, when she heard the voice of the Lord and met with Him inwardly, called the city of Samaria that they might meet with Him as she did, and Levi also, who gathered his colleagues to enjoy the Savior.

4.3.s.en: 5. "Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy mouth is sweet" [3].

4.3.0.en: If all the members of the Church are committed to double fruit, then the secret of this is "the lips like a thread of scarlet and the sweet mouth," that is, the believer is committed to bearing witness to the Savior through his lips and his mouth... and the meanings of these lips and this mouth are:

4.3.1.en: a. In the old days Rahab the harlot tied a cord of scarlet in the window as a sign of her faith in the Lord the Savior and her taking refuge in His blood that forgives sins and her confession of His ownership over her and her house, so she was rescued, she and all who were inside her house, from destruction. This is a living picture of the believer who ties everything that comes out of his mouth to the precious Blood, witnessing for the Lord by his words as by his works, so that he brings all into the house of God and saves all from destruction.

4.3.2.en: b. When the soldiers wished to mock the Lord they clothed Him with a scarlet robe, the sign of a king. But the Church, having been united with the King, her lips have become like a thread of scarlet; nothing comes out of them that is unbecoming to her as a queen or a bride of the heavenly King.

4.3.3.en: c. The lips of the bride are like a fine thread, which makes her mouth sweet; no wounding word comes out of it, it does not deceive nor flatter, but is gentle with all and loves everyone.

4.4.s.en: 6. "Thy cheek is like a piece of a pomegranate under thy veil" [3].

4.4.0.en: The garment of the high priest and his ephod were adorned with embroidered pomegranates (Ex 28:33-34; 39:24-26), and the Temple was adorned in various places with carvings in the shape of pomegranates (1 Kgs 7:18). So the pomegranate signifies adornment, with which the Church is beautified as the garment of the Lord Christ, the great High Priest, and the Temple in which His Holy Spirit dwells.

4.4.1.en: He assigned the pomegranate to the cheek because the cheek signifies the features of man, on which appear the signs of joy or sorrow, peace or distress; and the features of the Church are beautiful, gladdening and filled with peace.

4.4.2.en: He did not say "thy cheek is like a pomegranate" but "like a piece of a pomegranate," in order to show what is within it, for it is rich in seeds packed with sweet red juice, ever fresh, knowing no withering.!

4.4.3.en: Her cheek is like a piece of a pomegranate, filled with redness; the secret of her beauty is the blood of the Lord Christ which sanctifies her, so that there is no trace of defilement within her. This redness also signifies the soul's modesty and shame, for she does not conform to the people of this world in arrogance and brazenness of face.

4.4.4.en: As for her cheek being "under her veil," its secret is not shame before men, but the declaration of the truth of her glory that it is from within (Ps 45).

4.5.s.en: All of them shields of mighty men" [4].

4.5.0.en: The Lord often links the beauty of the Church with her striving, so that the believers understand that their beauty in Christ Jesus has as its secret also their lawful spiritual striving; so the cheek of the Church does not remain beautiful like a piece of a pomegranate without the neck set upright like the tower of David builded for an armoury, that is, without the living, upright, undeviating faith joined with striving.

4.5.1.en: Through this neck, which is faith, the face of the Church is lifted up to heaven and the Lord shines upon it with His light, making her live upright, not like the woman bowed down toward the earth (Lk 13:11-16), but standing upright, seeing in God the secret of her strength and her striving. She hears Him say to her: "I am thy shield" (Gen 15:1), and through Him she is protected from all the fiery darts of the enemy (Eph 6:16).

4.5.2.en: He likened her neck to the tower of David, for David represents the faith that fought Goliath the giant and overcame him, saying to him: "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts" (1 Sam 17:45). David the prophet declared in his Psalms that God is his refuge and the fortress of his life, and at the same time he does not cease to strive.

4.5.3.en: It was the custom of the mighty commanders to hang their shields on the tower in remembrance of their brilliant victories and to display their heroism; so the believers use this spiritual tower, which is faith, as the center of their victory in Christ Jesus and their triumph over the evil enemy.

4.5.4.en: As for the mention of the number of the shields, "a thousand," it refers to the nature of these weapons, for the number 1000 signifies the heavenly life, as though He says that the weapons of the Church are heavenly and spiritual, as the Apostle Paul says: "For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds" (2 Cor 10:4).

4.6.s.en: Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense" [5-6].

4.6.0.en: If the Lord Christ appears to the Church girt about the paps with a golden girdle (Rev 1:12), as He presents the Old and New Testaments as two breasts which the Church suckles and is nourished by, then the Church also, being the Church of Christ, has these two Testaments as two breasts by which her children are nourished.

4.6.1.en: The word of God contained in the two Testaments appears as twin young roes born of one mother, a reference to the completeness of the two Testaments together without distinction between them, for the Old Testament prophesied of the New Testament, and the latter unveiled the former and made it clear.

4.6.2.en: And we saw that the lily signifies the company of the believers who have become like the Lord Christ Himself, "the lily of the valleys" (Song 2:1), and it signifies the inner energies of man, his emotions and motives, which become food for the word of the living God!

4.6.3.en: In the face of this praise given to the bride for her inner insight, her modesty, her striving in unity of spirit, her work of preaching, her fruitfulness, her gentleness, her faith and her holding fast to the word of God... the bride declares to her Bridegroom that the secret of all this is the Cross of the Bridegroom and His resurrection; therefore she pledges before Him to go with Him to the mountain of myrrh, entering with Him into the life of suffering and being buried with Him in the tomb, and likewise to go with Him to the hill of frankincense, living all the days of her sojourn in unceasing prayer until the day of eternity breaks and the shadows of time flee away.

4.7.0.en: And the Bridegroom's expected answer will be:

4.8.s.en: "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no blemish in thee" [7].

4.8.0.en: It is as though He concludes His speech by saying: The speech would be long in describing the beauty of her who went out with Me into the fellowship of My sufferings and entered with Me into the life of prayer and fellowship. I perceive in you all beauty, because My love for you hides all your weaknesses, and My blood covers all your sins, bringing out every beauty with which I adorn you, so I see no blemish in you at all.

4.8.1.en: St. Jerome comments on this speech of the Bridegroom thus: [What is more beautiful than the soul that is called the daughter of God (Ps 45:10), that does not seek for herself outward adornment (1 Pet 3:2)? She believes in Christ, and as His Spirit is given to her, she takes her way toward Christ, who is her Bridegroom and her Lord at the same time, with great hope].

4.9.s.en: A call to work and striving:

4.9.0.en: "Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Faith (Amana), from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards" [8].

4.9.1.en: If at the beginning of the meeting with the Bridegroom the soul feels much consolation and rest, yet let her know that she is called to set out with her Bridegroom, in His company, to a life of lawful spiritual striving. It is noticed in this call, which the Lord repeats, the following:

4.9.2.en: It is a call to go out with the Bridegroom, for the spiritual war is the Lord's, on His account and in His name; if the soul goes out sheltering in Him she conquers and triumphs, without Him she knows only defeat.

4.9.3.en: If the call here is directed to the soul to go out with her spiritual Bridegroom from Libanus, as it came in the Septuagint, she is thereby called to set out through the life of prayer (because Libanus is derived from frankincense) to enter into confrontation with the lions and leopards, for the Christian life is not merely consolations in the chamber but also a fierce war against the evil powers of the spirit, against the devil and sin. Truly Peter longed to remain with the Lord on the mount of Transfiguration, saying to Him: "Lord, it is good for us to be here," but the Lord compelled him to come down with his two companions to face the events of the Cross.

4.9.4.en: And if the call is directed to going out with Him from Lebanon, which is a tourist country known for a life of luxury, then the heavenly Bridegroom calls the human soul to accompany Him, to go out of the easy life, the life of bodily comfort, and to face the struggle with the powers of darkness, while in the company of her Bridegroom, the conqueror of the lions and leopards.

4.9.5.en: As for the marks of going out, they are that she sets out from the top of faith (Amana), and through faith she is able to enter to the top of Hermon, to a life of deprivation and voluntary renunciation, practicing the Cross within her, by emptying herself through faith of the lusts and desires of the flesh, to live in a state of satisfaction in Christ Jesus alone. She says by faith with the Apostle Paul: "And having food and raiment let us be therewith content" (1 Tim 6:8), "I have learned both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil 4:12-13). And through this inner life, alive in Christ Jesus, the soul enters into the war to overcome by Christ Jesus the lions and leopards.

4.9.6.en: This is the starting point of the life of victory, which is a crossing with the victorious Lord from the beginning of faith to enter into a fierce war, indeed into spiritual victory and a crossing over to eternity.

4.9.7.en: St. Augustine commented on this call, declaring that the call here is not a crossing with Christ but a crossing to Him, that is, an entrance into union with Him to practice the spiritual married life, saying: [Cross over to me from the top of faith... for faith is the beginning of marriage].

4.9.8.en: St. Augustine also sees that it is a crossing of the bride to the heavenly Father through her union with the Bridegroom Christ, for he says: [She comes as the chariot of God, containing thousands of rejoicing men, going forward successfully and crossing this world to the Father, as her Bridegroom Himself, who crossed this world to the Father, brings her across: "I will that these be with me where I am," and by this they pass through the beginning of faith].

4.9.9.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees in these phrases a declaration of the increasing, limitless thirst of the bride to follow her Bridegroom, for he says: [Whoever arises directing himself toward God experiences continually a constant inclination toward increasing progress]. And he interprets the Bridegroom's phrase "Come with me from Lebanon Libanus, my spouse" thus:

4.9.10.en: [By this He meant: You have done well in that you have arisen with Me until now, and you have come with Me to the mountain of incense. You were buried with Me in Baptism unto death, but you arose and ascended in the fellowship of My divinity... And now rise up from here and come to two other summits, so that you grow and ascend continually through knowledge... Since you have attained this height, do not stop continuing to climb... This frankincense is the beginning of your faith by which you shared in the resurrection. It is the beginning of your advance to receive greater graces. Cross over and come from this beginning, that is, faith, and you will reach, but you will not cease from crossing over continually and continuing to arise].

4.9.11.en: The saint sees in her being called to cross over with Him "from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards" that man, whom sin had made a ravening beast like the lion and the leopard, has turned away from this nature... But the Bridegroom fears for His bride lest she relapse into sin again, therefore He calls her to go out always from the works of her old man; it is a call to continual striving joined with the life of faith...

4.10.0.en: At any rate, as her Bridegroom calls her to cross over with Him through the life of faith with continual striving and struggle against the spiritual beasts, she feels at times the bitterness of this struggle, so she lifts her inner eyes to Him seeking His help, and she hears Him answer her thus:

4.10.1.en: "Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck" [9].

4.10.2.en: At the beginning of her relationship with God He brought her into Lebanon, as the bridegroom does with his bride, for he often begins the married life with her in a tourist area far from the cares of life, where they get to know one another. But the married life will not remain so always; rather they must leave Lebanon to live in the marital home, striving and toiling... and so the Lord called her to go out with Him from Lebanon to face the lions and leopards in their dens. Or to go out with Him from mount Lebanon to a life of struggle against the works of the old man, which are like ferocious beasts.

4.10.3.en: In the midst of her bitter striving she groans within herself and her heart weeps, but He cannot bear her groaning and tears... so His heart is drawn to her, and her inward sighing captivates Him.

4.10.4.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa noticed that the Bridegroom here says "with one of thine eyes," because man has two kinds of sight, the outward sight by which he sees visible things, and the inward sight by which he beholds God... which is the heart. Here what captivates the heart of God is the tears of the secret inward sight.

4.10.5.en: As a heavenly Bridegroom He understands the heart of His bride; He cares for her at the time of her striving and her sufferings, and does not require words from her, but understands the language of her inner eyes... When Peter the Apostle fell into denying his Lord there were no words with which he could apologize, but the Lord knew what was in his heart through his tears. And when the sinful woman entered the house of Simon the Pharisee there was no room for speech, but the Lord, the searcher of hearts, said: "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much" (Lk 7:47).

4.10.6.en: And the Church has taught us to speak with the Lord in this language, the language of tears, at the close of every day, saying:

4.11.s.en: "Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens,

4.11.0.en: behold, they are as the eyes of servants unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress.

4.11.1.en: So our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us.

4.11.2.en: Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us: for we are many times filled with contempt, and our souls are many times filled with shame, which I repeat against them that are at ease, and the contempt against the proud. Alleluia" (Ps 122).

4.11.3.en: And the Lord's answer will be: I cannot bear your brokenness and your contempt. You have captivated My heart and all My love, so I do not call you servants but beloved ones. You are My brethren. You are My bride!

4.11.4.en: In a letter which St. Jerome sent to a blind priest in Baetica in Spain he spoke of the eye that captivates the heart of God, saying to him: [It is fitting for you not to grieve because of your deprivation of the two bodily eyes, in which ants and flies and creeping things share with all men, but rather to rejoice that you have the eye of which it was said in the Song of Songs: "Thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes." This eye beholds God, and Moses referred to it when he said: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight" (Ex 3:3). And we hear of philosophers of this world who put out their eyes so that their thoughts might turn entirely to the depths of their pure mind...].

4.11.5.en: God's heart is captivated by the language of the eyes broken before Him, as it is also captivated by the language of self-giving and obedience; for He says: "Thou hast ravished my heart... with one chain of thy neck." What is this chain that adorns the inner neck of the soul but the bearing of the yoke and obedience to the divine commandment? For it is written in the Book of Proverbs: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother: for they are a crown of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck" (Prov 1:8-9). So the bride is adorned by her accepting the instructions of her Father (God) with joy and gladness and her keeping the law of her mother (the Church)! In other words, she bears upon her neck the yoke of obedience, which is the easy yoke of Christ.

4.12.s.en: Now what have the sufferings of striving done to us?

4.12.0.en: If in the midst of sufferings we feel our weakness and lift our inner eyes in humility toward our God who is in our depths, we draw His heart and captivate His love by our contrition, and He declares the truth of our position, that we are in a position of strength, not weakness, and of glory, not contempt. If we groan through our sense of weakness, He yet confirms to us the truth hidden from our eyes: that our striving, despite all that appears in it of weakness, declares the sweetness of our love, and gives off a fragrance of ointments unique in their spices, for He says:

4.13.s.en: "How pleasant is thy love (thy breasts), my sister, my spouse?!

4.13.0.en: How much better is thy love than wine?!

4.13.1.en: How much better is the smell of thine ointments than all spices!" [10].

4.13.2.en: The words of the Bridegroom came matching the words of the bride in her praise of Him, but in a more wonderful and stronger form... How far are these words from the bride's saying:

4.13.3.en: "For thy (love) breasts are better than wine, because of the savour of thy good ointments..." (Song 1:2-3).

4.13.4.en: While we say to Him: "For thy breasts are better than wine," He says to us: "How pleasant is thy love (thy breasts), my sister, my spouse?! How much better is thy love than wine!" We commune with Him: "because of the savour of thy good ointments," but He says strongly: "How much better is the smell of thine ointments than all spices?!"

4.13.5.en: Wonderful is the Lord in His regard for us and in His praise of us, although the love which we carry is only a reflection of His love in us, and the fragrance of spices which we carry is only the fruit of His spices at work in us! How marvelous: He gives us what is His, then returns and ascribes it to us, and praises us for it and rewards us for it.!!

4.13.6.en: St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees the sublimity of the Church of the New Testament through the fragrance that breathes from her, for she is "better than all spices," surpassing the fragrance of every worship offered previously, for he says:

4.13.7.en: [The mystery of the truth accomplished through the message of the Gospel is alone sweet to God, and is reckoned more sublime than all the spices of the Law, for it is no longer hidden behind a symbol or a shadow, but its fragrance is breathed forth in a clear and open declaration of the truth. If one of the previous spices pleased the Lord as a sweet savour, the secret of its acceptance was not the loftiness of its material or its appearance which were used in the acts of worship, but the meaning which it declared through these acts. This is clear from the great saying of the prophet: "I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he goats out of thy folds... for I will not eat the flesh of bulls, nor drink the blood of goats" (Ps 49:9, 13)].

4.13.8.en: But now it is no longer animal sacrifices but the unique Sacrifice which the Father smells as a savour of acceptance... through this Sacrifice God smells all our worship and all our spiritual striving as a sweet fragrance "better than all spices."

4.14.0.en: Therefore in the midst of our bitterness because of our feeling of weakness, the Lord praises us without flattery or hypocrisy, but returns and speaks in more detail about the blessing of fellowship in sufferings with Him, or striving for His sake and in His name, saying:

4.15.s.en: "Thy lips, O my spouse, drop honey,

4.15.0.en: honey and milk are under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments is like the smell of frankincense" [11].

4.15.1.en: What does the Lord see in His striving, suffering bride? He sees her as the bee, of which it is said: "The bee is little among such as fly; but her honey is the sweetest of foods" (Sir 3:11). St. Gregory of Nyssa comments on this, saying: [The bee is loved by everyone and esteemed by all, for although her strength is weak she carries a heavenly wisdom and always strives to attain the life of perfection]. This is the secret of the honey which drops from the lips of the bride and the honey under her tongue, therefore the saint says: [It is fitting for us to fly over the meadows of inspired teachings, and to gather from each of them into our storehouses of wisdom. Thus honey is formed within us, as that sweet produce which is stored in our hearts as in a beehive, and through the various teachings storehouses are formed in our memory after the likeness of the waxen cells which do not perish. We must be like the bee, for her honey is sweet and her sting does not harm, busy in the important work of virtue. She is truly occupied in turning the toils of this life into eternal blessings, and offering her labor for the health of kings and herbs. So also the soul attracts the Bridegroom, and the angels admire her, who complete her strength in weakness through honored wisdom].

4.15.2.en: What else does the Lord see in His striving, suffering bride? He sees her as the holy land that floweth with milk and honey (Ex 3:8, 17).

4.15.3.en: The Lord presented His striving, suffering bride in the most wonderful picture, for if the Lord promised His people of old a land flowing with milk and honey to be for them a place of bodily rest and a place of bodily satisfaction and a center for worship upon it, then His bride in her turn becomes herself the Lord's place of rest; the Holy Trinity rests within her, and she overflows from the fruit of the Spirit with milk and honey which God and His angels desire and in which the saints rejoice, and it even overflows to unbelievers.

4.15.4.en: In the midst of the believer's sufferings the Lord sees his lips dropping honey and his tongue hiding honey and his breast filled with spiritual milk.

4.15.5.en: As for the honey which drops from his lips, it signifies the words of grace that come from the mouth of the believer, few, falling like drops (dropping), but sweet and delightful! They give the hearer a blessing and inward sweetness and rest in the soul!

4.15.6.en: As for the honey, it is like a hidden treasure "under the tongue" which the believer presents to others without ostentation or love of display... a treasure and food suited to the mature.!

4.15.7.en: What can this hidden honey be but the "word of God" the living, who was called the heavenly manna, whose type was the manna that came down upon the people of old, "and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey" (Ex 16:31). When Ezekiel the prophet ate the word of God he said: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness" (Ezek 3:3), and the psalmist described it thus: "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Ps 119:103), "the judgments of the LORD are true and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb" (Ps 19:9-10). Solomon the wise also asked us to enjoy eating the good word of God when he said: "My son, eat thou honey, because it is good" (Prov 24:13), "Pleasant words are as a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Prov 16:24).

4.15.8.en: At any rate, when the Lord speaks of His care for His people He assures them that He gave them honey as a reference to the sweetness of His gift, or the sweetness of His word in their mouth, for He says: "Thou didst eat fine flour, and honey, and oil: and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and wast fit for the kingdom" (Ezek 16:13), "with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee" (Ps 81:16), "He made him to suck honey out of the rock" (Deut 32:13). The honey of the word of God is the secret of the beauty of His people so that they are fit to become a queen, and the secret of her satisfaction and her being watered: He who feeds His people with honey returns and finds this honey of His hidden under the tongue of His bride, and so He rejoices in her.!

4.15.9.en: If the Lord presents His honey through the tongue of His bride to satisfy the mature, He fills her breast with unadulterated milk so that the children find for themselves a place in His Church and rest with His bride. And as St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [The man who knows how to speak with every kind of person and has under his tongue different powers of the divine word (honey and milk) is the one who is able to give each one what suits him according to his capacities at the right time].

4.15.10.en: We all know that man in the midst of his sufferings and afflictions forgoes his clothing, but the Bridegroom here smells the fragrance of the bride in the midst of her sufferings as the fragrance of pure prayer (frankincense)! He listens to her sighs and her petitions because she is in a state of suffering! He gives ear to her and answers her requests because she is broken-hearted! By this the believer, in his spiritual striving, puts off his earthly garments in order that the Holy Spirit may clothe him with the garments of heaven which do not wear out: "love, joy, peace..." (Gal 5:22). This is the work of the Spirit in the life of the suffering bride!

4.16.0.en: Finally, man often looks at himself in the time of affliction and thinks he is in a wasteland without inhabitant, barren without fruit, but the Lord sees the opposite, for He says:

4.17.s.en: "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse;

4.17.0.en: a spring shut up, a fountain sealed" [12].

4.17.1.en: It is as though He says to her: Remember the complete potentialities within you, you are a garden and a spring and a fountain, the potentialities of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, which are not revealed in you unless you accept sufferings and your back is bowed to the Cross.

4.18.s.en: Why was the bride called a garden inclosed and a fountain sealed?

4.18.0.en: 1. St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the garden contains different kinds of trees. Their fruit is bitter at first, but at the right time, when it ripens, it is sweet and beneficial, delighting all the senses... So the soul in her spiritual life, as the Lord Himself plants her and waters her, bears sufferings and toils and bitterness... and at the right time brings forth fruit that delights souls. 2. The saint speaks of the secret of her being enclosed, saying: [Our garden is enclosed on every side by the wall of the commandments so that no thief or ravening beast may steal into it. It is enclosed by the fence of the commandments so that no wild boar can approach it]. 3. If the garden needs a spring or a fountain, the spring must be shut up and the fountain sealed, and as the wise man says: "Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. Let not thy fountains be dispersed abroad, nor rivers of waters in the streets. Let them be only thine own, and not strangers' with thee. Let thy fountain be blessed" (Prov 5:15-18). So the divine inspiration commands us not to waste the waters of our fountains outside, in the streets, with strangers... And as St. Gregory says, when our inner thoughts turn aside toward sin (the stranger) we have lost the waters of our fountains and given them to strangers. [It is purity which seals this fountain so that it may be for its Lord].

4.18.1.en: St. Ambrose sees that the sealed fountain is Baptism, which remains sealed and shut if it is not usurped by deeds and declared by words. By Baptism we have become a paradise in which is the possibility of life and fruit-bearing, but a paradise inclosed, and a spring able to burst forth pure and sweet waters that water many but it is shut up, and a fountain sealed which if opened would burst forth springs of living water.!

4.18.2.en: We may think of ourselves that we are empty, but God sees within us a paradise and a spring and a fountain that it is not right to open except to Him, for He is the only Bridegroom of the soul, who has the right to enter the garden of the heart and drink the springs of His love! In other words, the soul as a bride is committed to remain in her virginity longing for the heavenly Bridegroom alone, opening to Him her heart and her feelings and her emotions and all her energy, as the chaste virgin awaiting her bridegroom (Mt 25), as a member of the Church of the firstborn.

4.18.3.en: St. Ambrose has a beautiful comment, for he says: [The Lord utters this saying to the Church whom He wants to be a virgin without defilement and without blemish. The fertile garden is virginity, which can bear much fruit having a good fragrance... It is a garden inclosed because it is surrounded on every side by the wall of purity. And it is a fountain sealed because virginity is the fountain and source of chastity, keeping the seal of purity preserved without decay, in which the image of God is reflected, where the purity of simplicity agrees also with the purity of the body].

4.18.4.en: St. Ambrose linked this seal with the mystery of the Eucharist, for he saw in Christ's speech here about the Church a commandment from the Bridegroom toward His bride who feeds on His most holy Body and precious Blood, keeping these Mysteries in her life sealed, not loosing them by works of evil and the loss of purity.

4.18.5.en: St. Augustine sees that this garden inclosed is the Church, for he says:

4.18.6.en: [Paradise is the Church as she was called in the Song of Songs, and the four rivers of Paradise are the four Gospels, and the fruit-bearing trees are the saints, and the fruits are their works, and the tree of life is the Holy of Holies, that is, Christ, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is freedom of will, for if a man despises the will of God he destroys himself, and then he learns the difference between sanctifying himself for the common good and what he does according to his own will].

4.18.7.en: And finally, many of the Fathers saw in St. Mary the Virgin "the garden inclosed," and in this she represents the virgin Church which is sanctified to the Lord alone. St. Augustine says:

4.18.8.en: [Christ Himself is a virgin, and His mother is also a virgin. Yes, although she is His mother she is still a virgin, for Jesus entered into her "the doors being shut" (Jn 20:19), He entered His new tomb hewn out in the solid rock in which no man before or after had lain (Jn 19:41). So Mary is "a garden inclosed... a fountain sealed." From this fountain flows, as Joel says (Joel 2:18), the river that waters the torrent from the briers and thorns, the briers of the sins which we committed and by which we were bound (Prov 5:22), and the thorns which choke the seed that the owner of the land sowed (Mt 13:7)...].

4.19.0.en: Therefore the garden inclosed or the spring shut up or the fountain sealed signifies the life which none enters but the Lord alone, who has the key of David, "he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth" (Rev 3:7). This life bears the precious heavenly fruits of the Holy Spirit, for He says:

4.20.s.en: "Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,

4.20.0.en: spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense;

4.20.1.en: myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:

4.20.2.en: a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon (frankincense)" [13-15].

4.20.3.en: What does the Lord find in us? He finds various kinds of fruits to eat such as the pomegranate, and sweet fragrances and spices and incense (frankincense) and materials used as good ointments and living waters to drink...

4.20.4.en: Thus the bride of Christ appears rich in everything: she has food that satisfies, and drink that quenches, and precious spices for adornment, and medicines for healing... Her Bridegroom and His friends rejoice in her. It is noticed in the mentioned phrases that the word "all" is repeated, so she lacks nothing, but is sufficient in everything. This is the expression which the Apostle Paul used in describing the believers, for he says: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work" (2 Cor 9:8). "We also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you, and to desire that ye might be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; that ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God; strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness" (Col 1:9-11).

4.20.5.en: The following are examples of the many plants which the soul carried within her, although I have already spoken of some of them in some detail. 1. An orchard of pomegranates: We saw the cheek of the bride like a piece of a pomegranate filled with redness, a sign of spiritual beauty through the blood of the Lord Christ, as well as a sign of modesty in gentleness and calm... She carries the beauty of the love of God and His gentleness...

4.20.6.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa speaks of the pomegranate tree, saying: [The pomegranate tree makes the thief despair of it, for its branches are fenced with thorns, and its fruit is covered with an exceedingly bitter and rough rind which protects it. But when the fruit ripens at the right time, as its rind is removed and you look inside it you find sweet fruit, attractive in appearance, delicious in taste like honey, with the flavor of wine... So it is fitting for us also not to be pampered in striving nor lovers of luxury in this life, but to choose the way of the chaste (self-controlled) hard life. By this thieves cannot approach the fruit of virtue, because it is fortified by the rough covering of self-control, and surrounded by a hard and stern way of life, as though it were thorns that prick whoever approaches it with an evil purpose. But at the right time we enjoy what the pomegranate offers of a mixture of delight in diverse kinds of fruit...]. 2. Camphire (henna): It was spoken of before; the bride uses it for adornment on the night before her wedding to prepare herself for the bridegroom with a sweet fragrance, and she dyes her hands and feet with it to make them red. 3. Spikenard: It is extracted from a small plant that grows abundantly on the Himalayan mountains, at a height of about 1100-1700 feet above sea level. It is a very costly ointment used in trade. With it Mary the sister of Lazarus anointed the feet of the Lord (Jn 12:13), and she or another poured it on His head six days before the Passover (Mk 14:3) as a sign of her love and thanks to Him. 4. Saffron: its flower is somewhat violet in color, with red veins, but the saffron itself is yellow in color, ground and mixed with olive oil to be used as an ointment. Saffron is used in food as a kind of spice, and it is also used in medicines. 5. Calamus: a wood with a sweet fragrance, from which an oil is extracted that is used in matters pertaining to the sacrifice (Isa 43:24; Jer 6:20). 6. Cinnamon: a kind of wood with a sweet fragrance, which some Easterners use instead of tea; it was used as one of the compounds of the holy oil for sanctifying Aaron and his sons (Ex 20:22), and it is still used as one of the ingredients of the oil of the Myron when it is cooked, and it was also used as a kind of medicine. 7. Finally the Bridegroom communes with her, saying: "A fountain of gardens, living waters, and streams from frankincense," for she carries within her her Bridegroom, the living Fountain who waters His plants and His vines inside His inclosed garden, who takes hold of her with streams that sweep away all that she has toward eternity...
